newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain bonos set to rise ahead of Dublin EU summit.
newsitem.headline: Spain bonos set to rise ahead of Dublin EU summit.

text.p: Spanish bonds, which rose to all-time highs on Wednesday, could climb yet further and force the spread to their German counterparts down towards 120/125 bps before the mid-December Dublin EU summit, a Reuter poll showed.

Five of 10 financial experts polled on Wednesday said they expected further narrowing in the spread before the summit, though a few said there was a risk the spread would first correct and widen after its such a dramatic compression.

"We calculated the fair value (of this spread) assuming Spain would definitely be in EMU (economic and monetary union) from the start. The result is something around 125 and 135 basis points," said Alfredo Urrutia, economist at Societe Generale in Madrid.
On Wednesday, Spain's long-term bond future reached an all-time high at 111.45, while the spread over German Bunds declined to a low of 131 before bouncing back to 140 bps.
On Wednesday, the spread between 10-year Bonos and German Bunds reached a record low, narrowing to 131 bps.
On Thursday at 0810 GMT it opened at 136 bps. It has shrunk from 330 bps at the start of March or from 500 in summer 1995.

Carmen Nuzzo, analyst at Salomon Brothers in London, was even more optimistic. She forecast the spread would contract to 75 basis points before the end of 1997, falling steadily to 125 in the first quarter of 1997 and to 100 bps within six months.
"We can't rule out market volatility, but what we are saying to our clients is that we expect a steady decline. So we suggest buying on every dip," Nuzzo said.
The market has bounded higher on expectations Spain will meet the criteria for membership of the planned European single currency on time, as economic data continue to show improvement.
Lower-than-expected October inflation last week fuelled expectations of further official rate cuts in the coming weeks.
"Friday's Bank of Spain repo is likely to be too early, but I am still giving a 40 percent probability to a fresh rate cut," said SocGen's Urrutia.
November data could be even better, analysts said.

Urrutia said the market is discounting a key money market rate of 5.75 percent in June next year and 6.5 percent by year end. It now stands at 6.75 percent, following the sixth interest rate cut of the year on October 3.
But some fear the market has already priced in all possible positive news.
"I think the spread could end the year above 140 basis points. Further reductions cannot be explained by fundamentals," said Henrik Lumholdt, economist at Bank of America in Madrid.
What is really driving the market are expectations of further progress in the convergence process.

"Until now the spread's trend reflected strong will. I'm not saying we did not have reasons to be optimistic but the spread did not completely reflect economic fundamentals," said Valentin Fernandez, economist at Credit Lyonnais Securities.
This means the market could turn even more optimistic if EMU convergence continues.

The European Union's monetary commitee, comprising national treasury and central bank officials, is expected to meet next week to try to secure a final blueprint for a stability pact ahead of next month's EU summit.
So far, tough German demands have blocked an accord, which would penalize members of the single currency who run up excessive national deficits.
"The market still is not completely pricing in the real chance that Spain will enter EMU from its start," Nuzzo said.
-- Madrid Newsroom + 341 585 8340
